Clarke et al. (2022): the fitted model

In the foraging task of Clarke, Irons, James, Leber & Hunt (2022, QJEP), 58 people selected all 40 targets on each trial, 20 of each of two types, in a feature and a conjunction condition. As in other foraging studies, people tend to collect one target type in long runs in conjunction foraging, and switch more freely in feature foraging. The paper’s abstract says 64 people were tested; the data have 58 (exclusions, still to be confirmed). With 87,760 selections it is the largest dataset here.

This page shows how to work with a fitted model: checking convergence, reading the posterior, accuracy and posterior predictive checks. The model is the default one: multi-level, Fourier-124 directions, the default priors, 4 chains of 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations.

Note: this page doesn’t fit anything. It reads a saved fit (clarke2022qjep_fourier124.rds) from examples/real_data/fit_models/fits/. It isn’t in the repository: to make it, run fit_clarke2022qjep.R in this folder (about 4 hours on a laptop), which saves it there. See examples/real_data/README.md.

Code: clarke2022qjep.R.

source("../../../functions/set_up_FoMo.R")
[1] "set_up_FoMo.R: random seed set to 65 (FOMO_SEED)"
source("../fit_models/fit_settings.R")

# the fit this page reads (made by ../fit_models/fit_models.R)
require_example_fits("clarke2022qjep_fourier124")

n_post_draws <- 5    # posterior draws for the posterior predictive check

1 The data

d <- import_data("clarke2022qjep")

d$stim |>
  summarise(people = n_distinct(person), trials = n_distinct(trial),
            items_per_trial = n() / n_distinct(trial), .by = condition) |>
  left_join(summarise(d$found, selections = n(), .by = condition), by = "condition") |>
  knitr::kable()
condition people trials items_per_trial selections
feature 58 1134 40 45360
conjunction 58 1060 40 42400

One random trial from each condition. Items are coloured by target type; the line is the order the targets were selected in.

plot_trial(d$found, d$stim)

How long people kept selecting the same target type before switching (runs): the main difference between the conditions.

plot_runs(compute_runs(d$found))

Per-trial statistics, used below to check the fitted model against the data.

trial_stats <- compute_trial_stats(d$found)

2 The fit

# the fit, and the data list it was made from (fit_fomo() stores it with the fit)
fit <- read_example_fit("clarke2022qjep", "fourier124")
sl <- attr(fit, "fomo_sl")

Population-level estimates (medians and 97% HPDIs) and convergence. R-hat and ESS are coloured green (good), orange (acceptable) or red (bad). At 1000 iterations this fit’s largest R-hat is 1.02 and its smallest bulk ESS about 200: fine for a walkthrough, but a published analysis should use 2000.

fomo_summary(fit, cond_labels = levels(d$stim$condition))

Rank plots of the five worst-mixing parameters. If the chains have mixed well, each chain’s histogram is roughly flat and they overlap.

plot_post_traces(fit)

3 Posterior

extract_post() turns the fit’s draws into tidy tables (one per group of parameters), which the plot_post_*() functions take.

post <- extract_post(fit, d$found, d$stim)
plot_post(post)

The same spatial parameters, shown as what each does to an item’s selection weight:

plot_post_spatial(post, show = "weights")

Each person’s distance and relative-direction estimates, over the population’s:

plot_post_per_person_spatial(post)

And each person’s class-transition probabilities: how likely they are to select each target type next, given the type they just selected. With two types each row of the matrix sums to one, so the columns come in mirrored pairs.

plot_post_per_person_cat(post)

4 Accuracy

The fit doesn’t store a prediction for every selection (save_selections = FALSE, the default), so predict_fomo() makes them from 200 posterior draws. Deterministic accuracy is how often the item the model judges most likely is the one selected; the probability of the chosen item credits being nearly right too. Chance (dotted) is 1 / items left; the nearest-neighbour rule (dashed) always picks the closest item, so the gap above it is what the model adds to proximity alone. This is in-sample accuracy, which overestimates out-of-sample accuracy.

# the fit doesn't store per-selection predictions (save_selections =
# FALSE), so predict them for a subset of draws
pred <- predict_fomo(fit, sl, n_draws = 200)
acc <- extract_post(pred, d$found, d$stim)$acc
plot_post_accuracy(acc, d$stim, d$found)

5 Posterior predictive check

Whole trials simulated from the fitted model (5 posterior draws: the dataset is large), compared with the data. The model doesn’t predict when a trial stops, so each simulated trial keeps as many selections as the observed one.

# whole trials simulated from the fit; the model doesn't predict when a
# trial stops, so keep as many simulated selections as the data have
sim_post <- sim_fomo(sl, fit, iter = n_post_draws)
extract_pred(sim_post, d$stim) |>
  semi_join(d$found, by = c("trial", "n")) -> found_post
plot_trial(found_post, d$stim)
sim_stats <- compute_trial_stats(found_post)
plot_trial_stats(trial_stats, sim_stats)
